context.title: With several agents running, the hard part is knowing who needs you and why
context.body: cmux lets developers run many AI coding agents side by side, and rings a pane blue when an agent needs input. That works for one or two agents. With five, the rings say where, not why: a permission prompt, a question and a failed test all look the same, and each one means switching panes, reading back, answering and switching again.
assumptions: I've read cmux's docs and README but haven't run it with many agents; the product may already do some of this.
Inline answers assume agents expose their prompt type and options through hooks, extending today's `cmux notify`.
Visuals follow a dark native-terminal style with cmux's blue attention ring. No cmux logo.
Repos, agents and output are fictional.

goals.title: Say why, not just where
goals.body: Permission, question or failure, with what the agent wants.

goals.title: Answer without switching
goals.body: Allow, reply or open the pane from one queue.

goals.title: Protect flow
goals.body: Oldest first, keyboard-first, and quiet when there's nothing to do.

jtbd: When several agents are working in parallel, I want to see which ones are blocked on me and why, and unblock them in seconds, so they keep going while I stay in my own work.

evidence.finding: When an agent needs input, 'the affected pane gets a blue ring and its tab lights up'; a panel collects alerts and Cmd+Shift+U jumps to the most recent unread.
Agents raise attention with `cmux notify` wired into their hooks, so richer signals (prompt type, options) are possible.
cmux is a native macOS terminal 'designed for running multiple AI coding agents in parallel', used by hundreds of thousands of developers.

evidence.step: The role is about AI workflows
evidence.finding: The founding designer will 'help design the most useful product for developers to do work with AI' and own the interaction model end to end.

approaches: A queue that says why each agent is waiting

ranges.title: Pane rings
ranges.summary: Today's pattern: a blue ring on the pane and tab.
cons: You switch panes to find out.

ranges.title: Notification list
ranges.summary: A list of alerts; each jumps to its pane.
cons: No sense of urgency or type.

ranges.title: Attention Queue
ranges.summary: A queue labelled by why each agent is waiting (permission, question, failure), with the agent's request and one-click answers; oldest first, keyboard-first, and an all-clear state.
pros: Unblocks agents without leaving your pane.
cons: Needs agents to expose prompt types.
Inline answers must be safe (e.g. allow once).

decision.title: Attention Queue: who needs you, why, and a one-click answer
decision.body: Range 3. A side queue lists every agent waiting on you, labelled as a permission, a question or a failure, with how long it has waited. Common answers (allow once, a reply, open the failing pane) happen inline, and the pane ring clears as the agent continues.
reasons: Developers run agents to stay in flow; switching panes to read back breaks it.
The type of wait decides the urgency, so it should be the first thing you see.
Keyboard-first matches how cmux users already work.
decision.tradeoff: Inline approvals could make it too easy to allow risky commands. I'd default to 'allow once', show the exact command, and never batch-approve.

depth.body: Built as a working cmux window with two agent panes and a side queue. Three moments: three agents waiting (a migration that needs permission, a question about renaming a label, and two failed tests), each with its request and answers; the permission answered inline, so the ring clears and the agent continues; and an all-clear state after all three are resolved. Items ease in, and motion turns off for people who reduce it.

validation.method: I'd watch five developers running three or more agents for an hour, log every switch to answer an agent, then test the queue.
hypotheses: Less time agents spend waiting on a human.
Developers run more agents in parallel.

metrics.name: Agent wait time
metrics.definition: Minutes from an agent's request to the user's answer.

metrics.name: Pane switches
metrics.definition: Switches made only to answer an agent, per hour.

metrics.name: Parallel agents
metrics.definition: Average concurrent agents per active user.

nextSteps: Dogfood with five agents in parallel for a week.
Define prompt types with agent hook authors.
Test the queue with five heavy users.
Design the same pattern for cmux iOS.
